full_judgment:
3. The plaint case, in short, is that, the petitioner as plaintiff filed SCC Suit No. 01 of 1996 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Khulna and asked to order the defendant out of the suit godown in which the defendant was a Monthly tenant. The starting rent was Taka 130.00 per mensem but later mutually increased to Taka 300.00 per mensem, the defendant paid the rent regularly but stopped payment of rent from the month of October and November, 1995. The defendant started paying in the rent control Court Khulna in Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 1996. He paid till December, 1995. Notice in section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendant as he was a habitual defaulter. The defendant (Opposite Party No.1) entered appearance and pleaded in writing that he was a monthly tenant under the original owner of the property-Murali Dhar Agarwala since 1959. He used to pay rent regularly. The defendant, according to local usage and custom, purchased the possession of the suit godown with another contiguous front shop in consideration of Taka 35,000.00 after the liberation of Bangladesh on 2-02-73. There was written contract entered into between the parties with certain conditions. Thereafter, the defendant began to pay the plaintiff Taka 130.00 as monthly rent from 1980 as the property was sold to the plaintiff by the owner and the plaintiff on 22-05-82 accepted the terms and conditions of the contract dated 02-02-73 on the back side of the rent receipt and bound himself with the original contract. In other words, it was an acknowledgment by the plaintiff. Thereafter the rent was increased to Taka 300.00 which he had paid till September 1995. He paid rent for October and November but the plaintiff did not give him receipts. When the defendant wanted to pay the rent for the month of December 1995 the plaintiff refused to accept. The rent was sent by post on 17-03-96 but he did not accept and he started depositing rent with the Rent Controller, Khulna in Miscellaneous Case No. 20 of 1996, as such, he was not a defaulter. The SSC Suit No.02 relates to two shops. The defendant started paying the rent to the Rent Controller after refusal to accept. The monthly rent is Taka 400.00. 

 5. Exhibit "ka" is the contract for sale of the possession, Ext. Kha is the rent receipt and on the back of it the landlord accepted the terms and conditions in the agreement in Ext. Ka. The main question that arises here is, that when a landlord sold possession of a premises to a tenant giving him the right to sell the possession is evictable or not. Mr Halder referred to 31 DLR (AD) 155. It is Shamsuddin Ahmed vs Mohd. Hassan and others. It is regarding the payment of advance rent to be adjusted monthly. He also referred to 14 BLD 528. It is Md Jashimuddin and another vs Ms Nurjahan Begum. It is also regarding payment of advance rent. He has yet referred to 15 BLD 119. It is Munshi Amiruddin Ahmed vs ,Begum Shamsunnahar. In these cases section 10, section 14 and section 23 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance were discussed and all of them are cases of advance payment of rent and hit by law. None of the above decisions has similarity with the instant case. 

 6. Mr Sk Razzak Ali, learned Counsel, appears on behalf of the opposite party and submits that the document is a valid one according to section 53A. "The contract though required to be registered has not been registered or where there is an instrument of transfer that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefrom by the law for the time being in force the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession other than a right expressly provided by the term of contract." He said that the very document cannot be used by the plaintiff but it can be used as a shield by the defendant. He also submits that the plaintiff is estopped by promissory estoppel by accepting the terms of the contract entered into between the defendant and the original owner Ext. Ka. He also submits that the defendant is not an evictable tenant. The contract of tenancy is collateral to the main contract of sale of possession therefore section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not applicable in this case. The section applies in the absence of a contract or local law or usage contrary to a lease of immovable property. But he says that the sale of possession of the property is customary among the business community of our country. So, the tenant will not come under the purview of this law. The trial Court came to a finding that the defendant is not a defaulter and the plaintiff does not require the property bonafide. He submits that the trial Court came to the finding by assessing the evidence properly. It is on record that the defendant started paying rent to the rent controller Khulna when he was refused. He proved by adducing evidence that he sent the rent by money order, but the plaintiff refused to accept it. 

 7. It is in evidence that the plaintiff has other business also and he ran the business with his employees. The defendant and his witness No.4 adduced that the defendant paid the rent of October and November but the plaintiff did not receive it. It is also in evidence that the plaintiff filed the suit almost after two months of filing the Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 1996 in which the defendant regularly deposited the rent. The defendant is on the premises for 20 years and he has never been a defaulter. The tenant who bought possession is not an evitable tenant according to the terms of the contract. He is not therefore treated as a tenant under Premises Rent Control Ordinance as tenant at will. Although he is liable to pay the rent but if he is in arrears with the rent he will be sued for the money and no eviction is applicable to him according to the provision of Transfer of Property Act. The plaintiff by accepting the terms and conditions of the contract entered into between the defendant and the original owner Agarwalla is estopped. It may be called waiver or forbearance on his part or an agreed variation or substituted performance it does not matter. It is a kind of estoppel. By his conduct he evinced an intention to affect their legal relations. He made in effect a promise not to insist on his legal right. That promise was intended to be acted on and was, in fact, acted on. He cannot afterwards go back on it and insist on the performance of the original contract.
